final_text: In InnoDB every secondary-index entry stores the row's primary-key columns, so the primary key's size is paid again in every secondary index. MySQL's docs: 'If the primary key is long, the secondary indexes use more space, so it is advantageous to have a short primary key.'
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 innodb-index-types: 'each record in a secondary index contains the primary key columns for the row' and the quoted sentence appears verbatim. Same fact as A-IG-06 (attached to L-0135); keep this one.

final_text: InnoDB caches index and table pages in its buffer pool as they are read and evicts least-recently-used pages when it needs room. By default MySQL saves the most recently used 25% of buffer-pool pages at shutdown and reloads them at startup to shorten warm-up.
note: Buffer-pool page: 'caches table and index data as it is accessed'; 'the least recently used page is evicted'. Preload page: innodb_buffer_pool_dump_pct 'default value is 25'; dump_at_shutdown and load_at_startup 'enabled by default'.

final_text: A query avoids reading table rows only when the index holds every column it needs (an index-only scan, helped by a covering index). Otherwise PostgreSQL fetches each matching row from the table, which means a lot of random access; even an index-only scan pays off only when most table pages are marked all-visible.
note: PG 18 docs: ordinary index scan 'requires fetching data from both the index and the heap'; heap access is 'a lot of random access'; index-only scan 'will be a win only if a significant fraction of the table's heap pages have their all-visible map bits set'. Added the visibility-map condition, which the original omitted.

final_text: REPLACE takes every column from the statement and sets any column you don't list to its default. Because it deletes the old row, it also fires DELETE triggers as well as INSERT triggers.
note: replace.html: 'the old row is deleted before the new row is inserted'; 'Any missing columns are set to their default values'. create-trigger.html lists REPLACE as an example under both the INSERT and the DELETE trigger events.

final_text: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE reports 1 affected row for an insert, 2 for an update, and 0 if the existing row is set to its current values. MySQL advises: 'In general, you should try to avoid using an ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE clause on tables with multiple unique indexes.'
note: insert-on-duplicate.html: 'affected-rows value per row is 1 if the row is inserted as a new row, 2 if an existing row is updated, and 0 if an existing row is set to its current values' and the avoid-multiple-unique-indexes sentence verbatim. Replaced the paraphrased reason with the doc's own sentence.

final_text: Flickr's published ticket server actually uses REPLACE INTO Tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a'); SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();. Because REPLACE deletes and re-inserts the single stub row, each call produces a fresh AUTO_INCREMENT id.
note: Flickr post shows exactly 'REPLACE INTO Tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a'); SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();'. Duplicates A-IG-09 (on L-0172, where the query is taught), so optional here.

final_text: In MySQL, INT is 4 bytes (unsigned max 4,294,967,295) and BIGINT is 8 bytes (unsigned max 2^64-1). When an AUTO_INCREMENT column reaches the upper limit of its type, the next attempt to generate a value fails. Flickr's ticket table uses bigint unsigned.
note: integer-types table: INT 4 bytes, max unsigned 4294967295; BIGINT 8 bytes, 2^64-1. example-auto-increment: 'When the column reaches the upper limit of the data type, the next attempt to generate a sequence number fails.' Flickr: 'id bigint(20) unsigned NOT NULL auto_increment'. Dropped 'works on any integer type' (not stated on the pages).

final_text: PostgreSQL never hands back a nextval value: it is not reused even if the transaction aborts, so sequences can have gaps and the docs say they 'cannot be used to obtain "gapless" sequences'.
note: PG 18 functions-sequence: 'the value obtained by nextval is not reclaimed for re-use if the calling transaction later aborts' and 'cannot be used to obtain "gapless" sequences' (quote matches).

final_text: MySQL 8.4 writes the auto-increment counter to the redo log on every change and to the data dictionary at each checkpoint, so it survives restarts; after an unexpected exit before the redo log is flushed, a previously allocated value can be handed out again. PostgreSQL sequences can pre-allocate values in memory per session (CACHE); values allocated but unused are lost when the session ends, leaving holes.
note: MySQL: counter 'written to the redo log each time it changes and saved to the data dictionary on each checkpoint'; 'if the unexpected exit occurs before the redo log is flushed to disk, the previously allocated value could be reused'. Original 'reuse ... is not guaranteed' read backwards. PG CREATE SEQUENCE: unused cached numbers 'will be lost when that session ends, resulting in "holes"'.

final_text: In PostgreSQL, a serial column is shorthand for CREATE SEQUENCE tablename_colname_seq plus a NOT NULL column default of nextval('tablename_colname_seq'), with the sequence owned by the column.
note: PG 18 datatype-numeric shows the equivalence: CREATE SEQUENCE tablename_colname_seq AS integer; colname integer NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval(...); ALTER SEQUENCE ... OWNED BY. Added NOT NULL.

final_text: Instagram ran PostgreSQL, and each logical shard was a Postgres schema (e.g. insta5) holding the same set of tables. Several thousand of these were mapped in code to far fewer physical servers.
note: Instagram post: 'Each "logical" shard is a Postgres schema in our system', example insta5; 'several thousand "logical" shards that are mapped in code to far fewer physical shards'.

final_text: PostgreSQL's docs warn that rows skipped by OFFSET 'still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient', which is why deep LIMIT/OFFSET pagination gets slow.
note: PG 18.6 queries-limit: 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.' Verbatim.

final_text: MongoDB's documented range-pagination example sorts explicitly: find({_id: {$lt: startValue}}).sort({_id: -1}).limit(nPerPage), carrying the last _id forward. Always add the sort (ORDER BY id in SQL) so each page continues exactly where the last ended.
note: cursor.skip page: printStudents uses db.students.find({ _id: { $lt: startValue } }).sort({ _id: -1 }).limit(nPerPage) and returns the last _id.

final_text: PostgreSQL warns that using different LIMIT/OFFSET values to select different subsets of a query result 'will give inconsistent results unless you enforce a predictable result ordering with ORDER BY'. Without a unique order, rows can repeat or vanish between pages.
note: PG 18.6 queries-limit: '...will give inconsistent results unless you enforce a predictable result ordering with ORDER BY.' Verbatim.

final_text: Keyset ('seek method') pagination works with filters and non-ID sorts. Sort on a deterministic key such as (sale_date, sale_id), filter with a row-values predicate on the last values seen, and back it with an index on the same columns. 'Paging requires a deterministic sort order.'
note: use-the-index-luke fetch-next-page: adds sale_id to index and ORDER BY, WHERE (sale_date, sale_id) < (?, ?); 'Paging requires a deterministic sort order.' verbatim.

final_text: The real trade-off of keyset pagination is navigation: 'you cannot directly navigate to arbitrary pages', which suits infinite scroll and batch iteration but not page-number UIs.
note: no-offset page: 'most notably that you cannot directly navigate to arbitrary pages'; 'this is not a problem when using infinite scrolling'.

final_text: A normal MongoDB collection 'stores the _id index separately from the documents'. Since MongoDB 5.3, clustered collections can instead store documents in _id order in one WiredTiger file.
note: Clustered collections page: 'A non-clustered collection stores the _id index separately from the documents'; 'New in version 5.3'; 'store documents in one WiredTiger file ordered according to the index specification'.

final_text: PostgreSQL tables are heaps: CLUSTER reorders a table by an index once, but 'when the table is subsequently updated, the changes are not clustered'. Keyset pagination is still fast there because of the B-tree index on the key.
note: PG sql-cluster: 'Clustering is a one-time operation: when the table is subsequently updated, the changes are not clustered.' Quoted fragment is verbatim.

final_text: ObjectIds 'are approximately ordered by creation time, but are not perfectly ordered': they have one-second resolution and are generated by clients whose clocks may differ. Sorting by _id is only roughly equivalent to sorting by insert time.
note: BSON types page: 'ObjectIds are approximately ordered by creation time, but are not perfectly ordered'; 'Only contain one second of temporal resolution'; 'generated by clients, which may have differing system clocks'.

final_text: Twitter's original Snowflake IDs were 41 bits of millisecond time, 10 bits of machine id and 12 bits of sequence. Twitter promised only that they are 'k-sorted ... within a reasonable bound (we're promising 1s...)'.
note: snowflake-2010 README: 'time - 41 bits', 'configured machine id - 10 bits', 'sequence number - 12 bits'; 'k-sorted' and 'within a reasonable bound (we're promising 1s, but shooting for 10's of ms)'. Ellipsis quote is faithful.

final_text: Elasticsearch's 10,000-hit cap on from/size is the index.max_result_window setting, not a hard-coded constant. Past it, Elastic recommends search_after (with a point in time) and 'no longer recommend[s] using the scroll API for deep pagination'.
note: Elastic docs: 'This limit is a safeguard set by the index.max_result_window index setting'; 'use the search_after parameter instead'; 'We no longer recommend using the scroll API for deep pagination.'

final_text: DynamoDB Query results come in pages of at most 1 MB. You pass the response's LastEvaluatedKey as ExclusiveStartKey in the next request, a cursor rather than an offset. A FilterExpression is applied after the page is read, so a page can be empty yet still return a LastEvaluatedKey.
note: AWS page: pages 'of data that are 1 MB in size (or less)'; 'LastEvaluatedKey ... should be used as the ExclusiveStartKey'; with FilterExpression 'a page can return zero matching items and still include a LastEvaluatedKey'.

final_text: In X API v2, older pages come from an opaque cursor: read meta.next_token and send it back as pagination_token (with max_results for page size). The docs advise using since_id for new data instead of paginating repeatedly.
note: X docs: next_token in meta; 'make another request with that token as pagination_token'; max_results = 'Results per page'; 'For new data, use since_id instead of paginating repeatedly.'

final_text: As of Oct 2026 the X API is sold as pay-per-usage with prepaid credits ('No subscriptions-pay only for what you use'), e.g. $0.005 per Post read, capped at 3 million Post reads a month before Enterprise.
note: Opened 2026-10-13: 'No subscriptions—pay only for what you use'; 'Posts: Read' $0.005 per resource; 'capped at 3 million Post reads per monthly billing cycle'. Pricing is volatile, so optional; keep the date.

final_text: String keys compare by the column's collation, 'a set of rules for comparing characters'; under a case-insensitive collation 'a' and 'A' count as equal. Strings compare character by character, so numeric-looking string IDs sort '10' before '9' unless padded to a fixed width.
note: charset-general: 'A collation is a set of rules for comparing characters in a character set' and the case-insensitive example treats a/b as equivalent to A/B. The page says nothing about numeric strings; that sentence is plain reasoning from character-wise comparison, not sourced to this page.

final_text: Martin Fowler observes that 'almost all the successful microservice stories have started with a monolith that got too big and was broken up', and that early on 'the premium of microservices is a drag you should do without'.
note: MonolithFirst: both sentences verbatim. Reworded the second to quote it exactly ('microservice premium' is not the page's phrase).

final_text: In MySQL InnoDB 'the clustered index ... stores row data' and is normally the primary key. A primary-key range read there really is one B+ tree descent plus a sequential walk of leaf pages, exactly as the teacher describes.
note: innodb-index-types: 'special index called the clustered index that stores row data'; 'Typically, the clustered index is synonymous with the primary key.' Range-walk sentence is reasoning from that.

final_text: On Linux, CLOCK_REALTIME (wall-clock time) is affected by discontinuous jumps, e.g. when NTP or an admin steps the clock; CLOCK_MONOTONIC is not, but it does not tell wall time. Time-based ID generators therefore detect a backwards step and wait or refuse, as Twitter's Snowflake does.
note: clock_gettime(2): CLOCK_REALTIME 'is affected by discontinuous jumps in the system time'; CLOCK_MONOTONIC 'is not affected by discontinuous jumps'. Snowflake README: 'Snowflake protects from non-monotonic clocks, i.e. clocks that run backwards.'

final_text: ntpd slews the clock only when the offset is under 128 ms and steps it when the offset is larger. Kernel slewing is limited to 0.5 ms per second, so each second of correction takes about 2000 s to apply.
note: ntpd 4.2.8 docs: 'slewed if the offset is less than the step threshold, which is 128 ms by default'; 'slew rate ... limited to 0.5 ms/s'; 'each second of adjustment requires an amortization interval of 2000 s'.

final_text: A write() normally lands in the OS page cache. Only fsync() flushes the file's modified data to the storage device, so it can be read back after a crash or reboot. That flush is the expensive part of 'save the counter on every ID'.
note: fsync(2): 'transfers ("flushes") all modified in-core data of (i.e., modified buffer cache pages for) the file ... to the disk device ... so that all changed information can be retrieved even if the system crashes or is rebooted.'

final_text: RFC 9562 (May 2024) says UUID versions that are not time-ordered, such as UUIDv4, 'have poor database-index locality'. It introduced UUIDv7, a time-ordered UUID built on the Unix-epoch millisecond timestamp, to fix this.
note: RFC 9562 (May 2024): 'UUID versions that are not time ordered, such as UUIDv4 ..., have poor database-index locality'; UUIDv7 allocates 'a Unix timestamp in milliseconds in the most significant 48 bits'.

final_text: PostgreSQL 18 provides uuidv7(), which generates a time-ordered UUID from a millisecond Unix timestamp plus a sub-millisecond part and random bits, alongside gen_random_uuid()/uuidv4() for random UUIDs.
note: PG 18 functions-uuid: uuidv7 'Generates a version 7 (time-ordered) UUID. The timestamp is computed using UNIX timestamp with millisecond precision + sub-millisecond timestamp + random.' gen_random_uuid/uuidv4: 'Generates a version 4 (random) UUID'.

final_text: In InnoDB, every secondary-index record contains the row's primary-key columns. MySQL's manual notes that a long primary key makes all secondary indexes use more space, so a short primary key is advantageous.
note: Same page and sentences as A-D-01 (confirmed). Duplicate fact on a neighbouring item; optional so the page shows it once.

final_text: OWASP recommends replacing enumerable numeric identifiers with random ones like GUIDs, but stresses that 'even with complex identifiers, access control checks are essential'.
note: OWASP IDOR cheat sheet: 'replace enumerable numeric identifiers with more complex, random identifiers'; 'However, even with complex identifiers, access control checks are essential.'

final_text: MongoDB's ObjectId timestamp has one-second resolution. The 5-byte random value is generated once per client process, and the 3-byte counter starts at a random value. Timestamp and counter are stored big-endian, so ObjectIds sort roughly by creation second.
note: ObjectId page: '4-byte timestamp ... measured in seconds since the Unix epoch'; '5-byte random value generated once per client-side process'; '3-byte incrementing counter ... initialized to a random value'; timestamp and counter 'big-endian'.

final_text: Flickr's published query is REPLACE INTO Tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a'); followed by SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();. REPLACE removes and reinserts the single 'a' row, so the auto-increment counter hands out the next value.
note: Flickr post SQL verbatim: REPLACE INTO Tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a'); SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();. MySQL replace.html confirms the old row 'is deleted before the new row is inserted'.

final_text: Flickr reports its two ticket servers drift out of sync - at the time of writing it had a few hundred thousand more odd-numbered objects than even-numbered ones - 'but this hurts no one'.
note: Flickr: 'The sides do drift a bit out of sync'; 'I think we have a few hundred thousand more odd number objects then evenly numbered objects at the moment, but this hurts no one.'

final_text: Flickr deliberately does not replicate between its two ticket servers: at that write volume 'replicating between the boxes would be problematic, and locking would kill the performance of the site'.
note: Flickr: 'At this write/update volume replicating between the boxes would be problematic' and 'locking would kill the performance of the site'.

final_text: When MySQL Group Replication starts in multi-primary mode and auto_increment_increment and auto_increment_offset are both still at their default of 1, it sets the increment to group_replication_auto_increment_increment (default 7) and the offset to the server ID, so each primary generates non-colliding auto-increment values.
note: replication-options-source: increment 'changed to the value of group_replication_auto_increment_increment, which defaults to 7, and ... auto_increment_offset is changed to the server ID'; 'only made ... if [both] each have their default value of 1'; not in single-primary mode. Made the variable and conditions exact.

final_text: InnoDB auto-increment values are never reused after a rollback, so gaps are normal. Under the default interleaved lock mode (MySQL 8.4), values stay unique and increasing across concurrent INSERTs, but the values a single statement gets may not be consecutive.
note: MySQL 8.4: rolled-back values are 'lost' and 'not reused'; interleaved is the default; 'auto-increment values are guaranteed to be unique and monotonically increasing across all concurrently executing "INSERT-like" statements', but 'the values generated for the rows inserted by any given statement may not be consecutive'. Original wording implied values are mixed out of order.

final_text: InnoDB writes the current maximum auto-increment counter to the redo log on every change and to the data dictionary at checkpoints, so the counter survives a normal restart and a restarted ticket server resumes where it stopped. After a crash before the redo log is flushed, a recently issued value can be issued again.
note: Same page: persistence sentence verbatim; caveat 'if the unexpected exit occurs before the redo log is flushed to disk, the previously allocated value could be reused'. For an ID service that caveat matters, so added it.

final_text: Twitter's 2010 Snowflake was a Thrift server written in Scala. Twitter has retired that open-source release (repository archived in September 2021); the internal version is described as a full rewrite on Twitter's infrastructure.
note: snowflake-2010 README: 'Thrift Server written in Scala'. master README: 'We have retired the initial release of Snowflake'; 'The Snowflake we're using internally is a full rewrite'; repo 'archived by the owner on Sep 18, 2021'.

final_text: Twitter's stated Snowflake requirements were 'minimum 10k ids per second per process' with a response time of about 2 ms plus network latency, IDs under 64 bits, and k-sorted ordering.
note: README: 'minimum 10k ids per second per process'; 'response rate 2ms (plus network latency)'; 'keep our ids under 64bits'; 'k-sorted'.

final_text: Snowflake promised IDs 'k-sorted' within one second, aiming for tens of milliseconds, rather than strictly ordered.
note: README: 'the id numbers will be k-sorted' 'within a reasonable bound (we're promising 1s, but shooting for 10's of ms)'.

final_text: Discord documents its snowflake as a 42-bit timestamp (bits 63-22, milliseconds since 2015-01-01), a 5-bit internal worker ID, a 5-bit process ID and a 12-bit increment. Its HTTP API returns these IDs as strings.
note: Discord reference table: Timestamp 63-22, 42 bits, 'Milliseconds since Discord Epoch, the first second of 2015'; worker 5 bits; process 5 bits; increment 12 bits; 'they are always returned as strings in the HTTP API'.

final_text: Sonyflake's default layout trades per-instance throughput for lifetime and machine count: 39 bits of time in 10 ms units (about 174 years), an 8-bit sequence (256 IDs per 10 ms) and a 16-bit machine ID (65,536 machines). Sonyflake v2 lets you change these bit lengths and the time unit.
note: README: '39 bits for time in units of 10 msec', '8 bits for a sequence number', '16 bits for a machine id', 'lifetime (174 years)', '2^8 IDs per 10 msec'. Version drift: v2 makes BitsSequence, BitsMachineID and TimeUnit configurable (defaults 8/16/10 ms), so added 'default'.

final_text: Google Spanner's TrueTime lets it assign monotonically increasing commit timestamps across all servers without global communication, so transactions appear in a serial order consistent with commit order.
note: Spanner docs: 'TrueTime enables applications to generate monotonically increasing timestamps'; 'This guarantee holds across all servers and all timestamps'; used for writes 'without the need for global communication'; 'the serial order is consistent with the order in which transactions can be observed to commit'.

final_text: TiDB's Placement Driver allocates timestamps (TSO) that always move forward: 46 bits of physical milliseconds plus an 18-bit logical counter for multiple timestamps within the same millisecond.
note: TiDB TSO page: PD allocates timestamps; 'The first 46 bits are the physical timestamp'; 'The last 18 bits are the logical timestamp'; 'always moves forward and never regresses'.

final_text: Amazon SQS standard queues are at-least-once: a message copy can occasionally be delivered again, and AWS tells applications to be idempotent. If ID ranges are distributed through such a queue, a redelivered range would produce duplicate IDs unless consumers deduplicate.
note: SQS page: 'you might get that message copy again when you receive messages. Design your applications to be idempotent'. Duplicate-range consequence is reasoning from that.

final_text: DynamoDB's UpdateItem can act as an atomic counter, but the update is not idempotent: a retried increment can overcount. For range allocation that only wastes a range, which is safe.
note: Atomic counters section: 'With an atomic counter, the updates are not idempotent'; positive increment 'can cause overcounting'; retry 'would risk updating the counter twice'.

final_text: Meituan's open-source Leaf ID service offers both models from this lecture: a database-backed 'segment' (range) mode and a snowflake mode taken from Twitter's algorithm, which needs a ZooKeeper address.
note: Leaf README: 'Leaf provides two ways to generate ids (segment mode and snowflake mode)'; 'The algorithm is taken from twitter's open-source snowflake algorithm'; leaf.snowflake.zk.address required. Useful pointer, not essential.

final_text: A common 32.768 kHz tuning-fork crystal is typically accurate to about +/-20 ppm at room temperature. Its error follows a parabolic curve with a coefficient of about 0.04 ppm/C^2, so accuracy drops at both high and low temperature extremes.
note: ECS Inc. (crystal manufacturer) page: 'typically ±20ppm at room temperature or roughly +25°C'; 'A common parabolic coefficient for a 32.768 kHz tuning fork crystal is 0.04 ppm/°C2'; 'decrease of accuracy at extreme high and extreme low temperatures'.
